Customs tariff-397. Pipe or tubes of iron or steel, n.o.p., with plain or processed ends, whether or not coated or lined: British preferential tariff, 12J per cent; most-favoured-nation tariff, 20 per cent; general tariff, 30 per cent.

I have been aware for a considerable time that representations were made to the former minister of finance in connection with the customs tariff relating to basic iron and steel products as well as iron and steel pipes and tubes. These matters were referred to the tariff board under reference Nos. 118 and 119, and certain recommendations were made by the tariff board in connection with pipe. The city of Welland happens to be a pipe manufacturing centre, so naturally I have looked at these proposed items with a view to ascertaining whether or not these tariff items might add to the large number of unemployed we have in that area now.
Under tariff item 384 the duty on skelp for use in the manufacture of pipes has been increased. The British preferential tariff has not been increased, but the most-favourednation tariff has been increased from 51 per cent to 7J per cent, and the general tariff has been increased from 5 per cent to 15 per cent. I am told that very little skelp comes in from Great Britain or the United States. The pipe mills in Welland are not integrated and they must buy their skelp. The fact is that the increase in the most-favoured-nation tariff of 2h per cent on skelp will in all likelihood increase the price of skelp, whether it is bought in the United States or at home in Canada.
I notice that the tariff board recommended one tariff item which would be the main or basket item relative to pipes or tubes of iron or steel. It would cover, wholly or in part, such pipes and tubes as come under 15 or more existing items. The recommendation of the tariff board was not to differentiate further in the size of pipe. The old item 397a had to do with pipe up to 10J inches and item 397b with pipe over 10J inches.

With the amendment brought in by the Minister of Finance the other night, he has in effect continued to make this differentiation against the advice of the tariff board. The new item 397 in the budget includes about 15 or more existing items and item 399 nullifies most of the protection given under item 397 for pipe 10J inches in diameter and larger, where the pipes or tubes of iron and steel and fittings and couplings are used in the transmission of natural gas to points of distribution, or in the transmission of crude oil.
I am told that all the pipe made in Welland by Welland Tubes Limited and much of the pipe made by Page Hersey which is in excess of 104 inches in diameter will come under the new tariff item 397, but this particular item will be largely nullified by item 399.
Having in mind the increase in protection given to skelp, I have prepared some tables showing the decrease in protection given to pipe under 10J inches in diameter and also pipe over 10J inches in diameter. I will give them in the three figures, namely British preferential, most-favoured-nation and the general tariff. Under the old rates they were 15, 224 and 30; under the present budgetary proposals they are 124, 20 and 30, so that the net tariff reduction is 24, 24 and zero. If we take into consideration the 24 per cent of raw material increase,-after all, the raw material, the skelp that the pipe mills have to buy constitutes about 65 per cent of their cost of production-instead of 24 and 2J and zero we would have 5, 5 and 24 as a reduction in protection. If we take the tariff board recommendation of 12J, 224 and 30 we have a net reduction of 24, 5 and 24 when we take the present budgetary proposals. Hence our manufacturers are worse off under these new proposals for pipe under 104 inches in diameter.
It is interesting to compare the proposed budgetary rates with the tariff board proposals and the old tariff rate on pipe of 104 inches in diameter and larger. The tariff board proposal was 124, 224 and 30; the budget rate is 10, 15 and 30. Hence the budget rate is under the tariff board proposal by 24, 74 and zero. In both cases there is a 24 per cent increase in the price of skelp, if skelp is sold in Canada up to the amount of the protection that is given. The old rate on pipe-I take it under 397b on pipe of 104 inches in diameter or larger-was 10, 15 and 20. This budget rate is 10 and 15, so that it is zero and zero. The present budget rate, of course, allows charges of 24 per cent on the skelp which would increase the raw material in the larger pipe so that in both cases we have these budgetary proposals which are detrimental to the manufacturer of pipe both 57071-3-217
Customs Tariff
under 10J inches in diameter and over 104 inches in diameter in Canada.
Taking into consideration, as we must, the 24 per cent increase in the tariff on skelp, the tariff board proposals give the best overall protection to the pipe industry; the old tariff the next; and the present budgetary proposals the lowest. The amendment announced by the minister has the effect of having one duty for pipe up to 10J inches and another for pipe over 10J inches in diameter when it has certain uses. This is contrary to the recommendation of the tariff board.
I understand that items 397 and 399 will apply to the great volume of pipe admitted into Canada. Without the amendment to item 399 I think our pipe manufacturers in Canada might have had fairly tough competition from foreign producers. Manufacturers of the larger pipe will not be as well off as they were before. I know that in Welland under the old tariff item it was difficult enough for the pipe manufacturers making large pipe to get orders. The new Welland Tubes Limited plant which was established under the former government cost many millions of dollars and makes all large diameter pipe. Page Hersey Tubes Limited also makes considerable pipe over 104 inches in diameter. I hear rumours that the former plant is to close down for a period of six months. I am not against a lower duty on pipe but I am against a lower duty on pipe when this government is at the same time raising the cost of production of pipe. The whole matter seems to be haphazard and discriminatory to my mind.
It seems to me that those who build oil and gas lines have monopolies in their particular fields and regions, but they are given very favourable consideration under item 399. I feel that this will put many Canadian workmen now working out of work. The pipe manufacturers claimed that they should have the same protection on all sizes of pipe in order to develop the industry. I know that much of this larger pipe has been admitted into Canada from the United States, Great Britain and Germany. I understand that Germany comes under the most-favourednation tariff. I do not know how much more pipe will come into Canada because of this decrease of duty on the smaller pipe and also because of the increase in duty on skelp for the larger pipe but I think in the city of Welland this will tend to increase the number of unemployed. The manufacturer of the larger pipe involves a new industry which is just getting started. I would personally like the government to adopt the recommendation of the tariff board rather than to reduce these duties, particularly since this might put a

Customs Tariff
number of our men out of work. I would much prefer to see our men employed rather than having much of the pipe imported while our men are walking the streets and in Welland we certainly have a number of unemployed men, and this applies to the pipe industry. Granted, Page-Hersey has recently been working steadily because of the new pipe lines coming into operation in Ontario, including the trans-Canada pipe line. However, I understand that the larger mill making the big inch pipe might have to close down for six months for lack of work. I do not for one moment mean that if they got an order they would not start operations right away, but the future does not look very bright for the large pipe manufacturers.
I would like to ask this government not to increase the cost of production of pipe, particularly when a blanket or across the board tariff for pipes of all sizes is not apparently being considered.

speechtext:
The discussion
seems to have dealt with items 397, 399 and 384 together, and perhaps it would be better if, for that reason, I dealt with all three together in my remarks.
The tariff at the present time has two relevant items; 397a, pipe not more than 104 inches in diameter, and the rates are B.P. 15 per cent; M.F.N. 224 per cent; general, 30 per cent. I may say at once to the hon. member for Ottawa West that that is the origin of the 104 inch diameter which is mentioned in the amendment which will shortly be introduced on item 399. The other item in the present tariff is 397b, pipe more than 10J inches in diameter, and the rates are B.P.,
10	per cent; M.F.N., 15 per cent; and general 20 per cent. It is important to bear in mind that there has been a drawback of 50 per cent provided in the case of pipe used for gas transmission lines.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, I will deal with that. In addition, remissions have been granted on pipe used for the construction of
011 pipe lines. That is the situation as we find it at the time of the tariff board inquiry. Now the tariff board conducted its inquiry and made certain recommendations. As has been suggested already, the resolution contains certain departures from the recommendations of the tariff board and, I submit, for good and sufficient reasons. It should be borne in mind that these are items which, under the terms of GATT, had to be negotiated with the United States, and try as we might we had no chance of coming out of these negotiations with the recommendations of the tariff board inviolate.
Would the minister indicate what he did trade, finally, in that respect?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is not customary to indicate the various stages in the bargaining. We might have to bargain again with 57071-3-2174
Customs Tariff
the United States at some time, and I think the hon. gentleman will realize that the practice in this respect is a sound one-not to attempt to retrace the various stages in the bargaining. But we did the best we could in the course of the negotiations and I think that in the event, having regard to the fact that there were bargaining and negotiating on both sides for quite an extended period, the result, though not entirely of our choosing, can be regarded on the whole as reasonably satisfactory to both sides.
To turn now to item 397 in the resolution which covers pipes or tubes of iron or steel not otherwise provided, with plain or processed ends whether or not coated or lined, here I intend to confine my comments to the rates under the British preferential and the most-favoured-nation columns because the general rates have, I think, only academic interest. The tariff board's recommendation with respect to pipes and tubes of iron or steel was British preferential, 124 per cent; most-favoured-nation, 224 per cent. The resolution now before the committee contemplates the following rates: British preferential, 124 per cent; and most-favoured-nation, 20 per cent.
It will be seen that we have emerged from these negotiations with the same British preferential rate, and a reduction of 24 per cent in the most-favoured-nation rate. I am going to make a comment a little later about that 24 per cent. Perhaps I might just say now before I return to the item on skelp, that this reduction of 2J per cent as compared with the tariff board's recommendations is offset by the 24 per cent reduction in the rate on skelp under the present resolution as compared with that recommended by the tariff board.
Before the minister leaves item 397-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have not left it yet. Under the general purpose pipe item, 397, the British preferential rate proposed is that recommended by the tariff board, that is 124 per cent. I wish to make that quite clear. And I have stressed the fact that the reduction on the skelp item-the material- of 24 per cent offsets the reduction of 24 per cent in the most-favoured-nation rate on the pipes and tubes under item 397. The effect of our proposal as compared with the recommendation of the tariff board is, first, to increase the effective margin of protection under the British preferential tariff and, second, to retain the effective margin of protection under the most-favoured-nation tariff. That is the net result of the change.

Customs Tariff
That is all I propose to say on item 397 and now, perhaps, the hon. member for Ottawa West might wish to ask his question.

I take it that the minister does not, of course, suggest that the 2J per cent difference on skelp between what was recommended and what he has brought in under the resolution is the equivalent of 2J per cent duty on the finished article? I am sure he will not want to leave that impression.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not entirely, and not in terms of dollars and cents. Nevertheless I think the hon. gentleman will agree that basically it maintains the difference that exists between the rate on the incoming material on the one hand and on the finished product on the other hand, in a tariff sense.

Before we leave item 397, I have just one other question. The minister has not dealt with the change of wording. What he has said by way of explanation of item 397 is weakened by the fact-and I would ask him to comment on this-that the item is no longer applicable to the vast majority of the pipes and tubes, because of the language used in item 399. Formerly, item 397 included oil pipe lines, but it no longer does.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Item 399, as I will say in a moment, sets up a new and special item for pipe lines, and pipe lines alone.
No; on 397, what I had in mind-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On 397 I thought, from the way in which the hon. gentleman started out, that he was going to talk about the change in wording in relation to fittings-
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -because they are dealt with now under item 400.

My point was that he compared it with 397a, which previously covered a large percentage of the total tonnage of pipe manufactured in this country. Because of the changed wording, it will now cover a relatively small percentage of the total pipe manufactured in Canada. That is the point I wish to make. Item 397 is no longer applicable to pipe used in oil pipe lines; whereas formerly it covered all oil pipe lines.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is true. That is the point I was dealing with. Item 399 is the new item which now deals with pipe for pipe lines. Item 397 remains the basic item dealing with pipes or tubes of iron or steel not otherwise provided, and we have taken out of the general description the tubes

or pipes, fittings and couplings, in 399 used in the transmission of natural gas to points of distribution or in the transmission of crude oil.

I do not think I am making myself clear to the minister. What I want to get at is this. The effect of changing the language in item 397 as compared with the former item 397a is to make this item, which the minister spoke of as the basic item, no longer the basic item. As it existed, the basic item covered a very large percentage of the total pipe manufactured in this country. Under the new language it has become applicable to only a relatively much smaller percentage of the total pipe manufactured in Canada. That was the point I wished to establish.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, item 397 covers all the pipes and tubes-
Not otherwise provided for.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -that the former tariff items 397a and 397b covered, with the exception of the pipes or tubes now proposed to be covered in 399. Items 397 and 399 cover the totality of pipes and tubes as did 397a and 397b under the old tariff.

Yes, that is correct. Going on from there, the point I want to establish is that under the old item 397a there was this higher tariff that the minister concerned himself with a moment ago. Item 397b was a lower item which, as I indicated, until very recently covered the pipes and tubes not made in Canada. That was the effect of it. By changing the language of item 397 the minister has now made it applicable only to certain limited pipes and tubes; whereas formerly it covered a very large percentage of the total pipe manufactured in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, my hon. friend and I were on common ground that 397 and 399 in the resolution cover the totality of pipes and tubes as did 397a and 397b in the old tariff.
That is correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Now without going too far off the line of argument or remarks that I was about to follow, let me just say here and now, Mr. Chairman, that in the amendment I am proposing to ask one of my colleagues to introduce to item 399 the rates will be for pipes or tubes of iron or steel more than 10J inches in diameter, and fittings and couplings therefor, B. P., 10 per cent; M.F.N., 15 per cent; general tariff, 30 per cent; whereas, under the old item 397b, which covered pipe more than 10J inches, the B.P. and the M.F.N. rates were just the same, namely 10 per cent and 15 per cent respect-

ively. Therefore, we have retained in item 399 in the amended form now proposed the hitherto effective B.P. and M.F.N. rates with respect to pipe more than 10J inches in diameter.
Now, Mr. Chairman, having said that, perhaps I should go on with the remainder of the explanation of item 399. Item 399, Mr. Chairman, as you will see, covers pipes or tubes of iron or steel and fittings and couplings therefor, for use in the transmission of natural gas to points of distribution or in the transmission of crude oil. These are the pipe lines, whether for transmission of gas or crude oil. The tariff board made a recommendation here, Mr. Chairman, and associated with the rates they recommended a proposal for a 50 per cent drawback. They recommended a B. P. rate of 12J per cent and an M.F.N. rate of 22J per cent. If you apply to that the drawback of 50 per cent which they recommended, you have effective net rates recommended by the tariff board of 6-J per cent B.P., and 11-i per cent M.F.N.
The budget proposal is that the rates be 10 per cent B.P., and 15 per cent M.F.N., so that the hon. member for Welland must see that what is recommended in the budget proposal is an effective increase in the effective tariff rates on the gas pipe lines recommended by the tariff board. I think, if I may say so to my hon. friend, what he overlooked in his argument was the existence of the drawback recommended by the tariff board as well as the fact that there has existed until now a 50 per cent drawback on pipe lines used for gas and a remission on pipe lines used for transmission of crude oil.
With respect to oil pipe lines, Mr. Chairman, the tariff board recommendation was for tariff rates B.P. 12J per cent; M.F.N., 22J per cent. The budget proposal is as follows: B.P., 10 per cent; M.F.N., 15 per cent; and on both B.P. and M.F.N. accordingly there is a reduction proposed in the resolution as compared with the tariff board report.
Just to recapitulate as briefly as can be, Mr. Chairman, as to pipe for pipe lines, the situation is as follows: On pipe used in gas pipe lines the tariff board recommended the continuation of the 50 per cent drawback of duty which was formerly in effect. On pipe used in oil pipe lines the tariff board made no specific recommendation in reference to drawback. However, on substantial quantities of pipe used in oil pipe lines, remission of duties has been permitted under the Financial Administration Act. That has been going on now for years.
Tariff item 399, as introduced in the budget, proposed a British preferential rate of 10 per cent and an M.F.N. rate of 15 per cent on all pipe used in gas or oil pipe lines. Since
Customs Tariff
the budget was introduced, representations have been received from the pipe industry pointing out that-this is the pipe industry that the hon. member for Welland was referring to-the item as introduced would cover pipe of all diameters. It is with those representations in mind that I am putting forward the amendment to item 399 in order to limit the item to pipe over 10J inches in diameter.
I remind my hon. friend that the 10J inches diameter comes from old tariff item 397b. It is now a well-established point of differential in the diameters of pipes for this purpose. The effect of this change will be that all pipe 10J inches or less in diameter will be dutiable under tariff item 397 which, as I have explained, retains the effective margin of protection between the rates of duty on pipe and on skelp recommended by the tariff board under the M.F.N. tariff and somewhat increases the effective margin of protection under the B.P. tariff.
With respect to pipe over 10J inches in diameter used in gas and oil pipe lines the British preferential tariff will be 10 per cent and the most-favoured-nation tariff will be 15 per cent. Under the tariff board's recommendations on gas pipe lines the effective rates would have been British preferential, 6J per cent, and most-favoured-nation, 11J per cent on most of this pipe, so that the item now proposed represents substantially more protection than would have resulted from the tariff board's recommendations. I think the hon. member for Welland must recognize that. On pipe used in oil pipe lines it would be difficult to resist requests for remissions of duties to the extent provided by the drawback item recommended by the tariff board on pipe for gas pipe lines, in which case the rates now being recommended would again provide significantly more protection to the pipe industry.
I have tried to make clear the effect of items 397 and 399 and perhaps at this point it is appropriate that I should say perhaps a brief word about skelp which is the basic material in item 384.
I have one or two questions I want to ask. Would the minister prefer me to ask them now?

I gave the reference to that a few minutes ago, page 43 of their report.

Coming to the drawback item applicable to the minister's argument, I take it that he was referring to 1018a. I think that is right. I wanted to point out one or two facts to the house that I think are relevant. The first is that that drawback item was only applicable to pipe 16 inches or more in diameter. That means that in effect it was only applicable to pipe not made in Canada. They could just as easily have used the language, "of a size not made in Canada", because 16

inches was the largest size made in Canada in 1955 when that drawback item was put in the tariff, as I understand it.

speechtext: With respect, I think my friend is in error there. If you look at page 40 of the tariff board report you will see that under 1018b the size of more than 16 inches in diameter applies only to pipes or tubes electrically welded. It was confined to that.

That is my whole point. The type of pipe used in the transmission of gas is electrically welded and the limitation of 16 inches is the same as saying, "of a size not made in Canada." That was my whole point. The drawback item was specifically made applicable to a size not made in Canada, and that is my understanding of the matter.
That does not deal with the other type of seamless pipe which is used as oil country goods. That same argument was not applicable to it. It did not have that limitation which was equivalent to "of a size not made in Canada." I should like the minister to address himself to that point. -pipes of the seamless type are now made in Canada by Page-Hersey up to and including seven inches in diameter; pipes welded (by various processes) actually are manufactured at present up to 16 inches and in the near future will be produced up to 36 inches in diameter.
My question is, if the tariff board attempts to give advice why do we stick to the old nomenclature in so far as some of these changes and departures from the tariff board recommendations are concerned? That is one point.

Mr. Chairman, I made some reference to this item when I spoke in the budget debate. The minister introduced it in his budget speech of June 17 and he said this was just a weeny bit of a tariff change. The Financial Post, in an article, subsequently estimated that the effect would only be to add perhaps three cents a pound to the cost of imported British cloth. But I pointed out at that time that to me the significance of the item was that it indicated a trend, a desire and an intention. I said that beyond that, and maybe more important than that, it would probably cast quite a chill on the forthcoming commonwealth conference because we were in this very small way adversely affecting an export from Great Britain-an export which happens to be Britain's principal export to Canada.

Customs Tariff
We had a visit from the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom. I heard all members of this house, and particularly members on the Conservative benches, cheering and applauding the Prime Minister of Great Britain when he came to this North American continent and was beyond everything else advocating that we should have economic interdependence, freer trade and lower tariffs. It was just four days later that the Minister of Finance brought in this somewhat chilling trade item-the budget papers in so far as this very important customer of Canada is concerned. As I see the change, it is not something particularly significant in itself-three cents a pound on cloth. I cannot for the life of me see how that would give anybody here a "fighting chance", as some people have said, for survival. As a matter of fact the tariff board itself looked at this, as we imagine they would, very carefully. They had previously considered it, but the new government forced them to look at it again. I just want the committee to be very clear about exactly what the tariff board had to say with regard to the possibilities open to them in this area. On page 42 of their report, with respect to wool fabrics, the board says this:
Whether or not the Canadian taxpayer should further assist by increased tariff protection the domestic wool cloth industry is debatable, unless, of course, it be on the grounds of national security.
This is the point I want to make. The tariff board recommended this rather nominal increase more or less under pressure from the government to give the matter reconsideration. I said the increase was not significant in itself, but it is very obvious in reading the report of the board that a policy with respect to protection or otherwise for this industry having regard to Canada's other advantages in trading of other products is doubtful, and the board, in its report on page 43, says this:
Apart, however, from the question of security, in respect of which cost to the taxpayer in peace presumably would not be a prime consideration, the matter of the maintenance in a healthy state of a wool cloth industry in Canada seems essentially one of high policy.
In other words, a decision of this nature rests upon the government. It is the government which must decide whether or not a three cent increase per pound is to be followed by a further increase of substance which might prevent the perhaps inevitable erosion that was predicted not only in this report of the tariff board but in the former report also.
I am simply going to say that I think there has been considerable ineptitude in the timing of the government in its attitude

toward this question. They profess to be the party which has the highest regard and consideration for imperial preferences and for special conferences and trade within the commonwealth. We all recall that there was a bit of a muff just prior to the Mont Trem-blant conference last autumn when this reference to the tariff board respecting woollen goods was made within a few days of the discussions between members of this government and their counterparts who came here from Britain to discuss the opportunity of widening trade.
Now we are again to have a commonwealth trade conference held in this country, and it is a great honour to have it here. But our government has attacked a trading item with Britain which happens to be that country's biggest export, and I suggest that this is an item worthy of very serious consideration by this committee and by the government.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman may I be allowed just a few words to call the attention of the house to the fact that the constituency of Joliette-l'Assomption-Montcalm is one of Canada's largest textile centres. In so far as that industry is concerned, the city of Joliette is one of the most important centres in this country. Indeed Pinatel Piece Dye Works and Consolidated Textiles Limited operate large mills in this community, employing large numbers of workers.
I congratulate the Minister of Finance for having raised the tariff on woollen imports from abroad. This will substantially assist the textile industry of this country. I urge him to continue that policy in order to encourage the textile industry and, of course, the workers themselves. As it is, the textile industry has been defined as an ideal industry for this country since, (a) it is at least 50 per cent Canadian owned and (b) it employs the largest number of workers over the winter, thereby reducing seasonal unemployment, (c) it provides goods of a highly necessary character,
(d)	it may be set up in areas which are not as highly developed as others and, finally, it uses Canadian raw materials.
Once again I congratulate the Minister of Finance for the step he has just taken with respect to woollen goods from abroad.
(Text):

Mr. Chairman, I was not aware that it was necessary to adhere strictly to the tariff changes, and I had prepared what was to have been my maiden speech in

defence of the woollen industry in the district of South Waterloo. However, I would agree with the ruling of the chair, and withhold my speech until a later occasion when I will be able to deal with the subject matter in a more extended way.

Would the Minister of Finance indicate what representations he has received from Great Britain since he announced in his budget speech that he had this present intention? We have certainly read some interesting comments in newspapers of importance in Britain, and they did not seem to think that it was a very promising inauguration or preparation for the conference on trade that is about to take place in Montreal.
Such important journals over there as the Financial Times, the Yorkshire Post, the Economist and others have commented upon the minister's intentions very bitterly, inasmuch as an opportunity is obviously being cut off for consultation on the lines of improving trade between one country and the other.
I do not wish to reiterate some of the things which are already on record in Hansard, but I think the hon. member for Mount Royal during the budget debate contributed some very important quotations from some of the most influential journals of the United Kingdom, and it is obvious that they are not taking this in good spirit. I wonder if the minister would indicate just what representations the government has received, and his view as to the extent to which it is likely to contribute to good feeling and effective bargaining at the commonwealth conference we are to have in Canada next month. This is likely to reduce the effectiveness of good feeling and bargaining at the conference that we are to have soon, in fact next month.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the difficulty
about that is that we are opposed to this particular resolution and since we take that position we wish to establish the reason why we are opposed to it, and I do not think that can be done in the five minutes that are left tonight. This I think is the place to do it, Mr. Chairman, because we have already been informed this session that if we have any general observations to make we should make them on the resolution. This I would like to do at this stage, but I certainly cannot do it in five minutes. However, I do want to indicate in the time that is available some of the reasons why we will not be able to support this particular resolution.
The minister has said that it is a very modest, very small increase. If it is a small increase, it is not going to do very much to help the Canadian woollen industry. The minister might also have said that this increase applies only to British imports and has no effect on the most-favoured-nation clause and therefore on other imports. As it happens, and as the minister knows, the British have not even been holding their share of this market; whereas imports from other countries, more particularly from Italy, have been increasing.
We know that the minister and the government are negotiating to maintain the margin between the British preferential rate and the M.F.N. rate and, as he has already indicated to us this afternoon in connection

Customs Tariff
with another item, in that process of negotiations the proposal which they make may not come out inviolate and therefore for that reason and for a good many other reasons we are not happy about this resolution.
It may not be enough of an increase to do very much for the woollen industry but it has been enough to cause a great deal of disturbance in the United Kingdom, as my hon. friend has pointed out, at the very eve of a commonwealth economic conference which will be dealing with trade matters. It seems to me to be a pretty unfortunate essay in international economic policy vis-avis the United Kingdom at this time when we are proposing to interfere with the exports from the United Kingdom, on the eve of this conference, of a commodity which represents her largest export to this country, I think something like $35 million worth of goods.
There has been abundant evidence, as my hon. friend from Kenora-Rainy River pointed out, that while this may be a modest increase it has not been considered in its implications as such on the other side. Even the high commissioner of the United Kingdom, who is a discreet individual and a diplomat and normally would not have very much, if anything whatever, to say on a matter of this kind, is quoted in the Vancouver Sun of July 21, 1958, as follows:
Britain's offer of free trade with Canada is still open, United Kingdom High Commissioner Sir Saville Garner said in Vancouver today.
It's on the table. Any time the Canadian government wishes to discuss it they'll find a ready response in the United Kingdom".
When he was asked about the British reaction to Canada's increase in wool tariff, which was announced in the minister's budget, he replied:
"No comment".
This is the kind of comment you would expect from a discreet and experienced diplomat. Apparently his feelings were too much for him because he added:
We were inevitably disappointed-especially at a time when the United Kingdom is trying to work up enthusiasm to come into this market.
And, Mr. Chairman, they have been encouraged by this government to work up excitement and enthusiasm. The Chairman of the National Wool Textile Export Corporation of Bradford, Yorkshire, states in regard to this increased duty:
The Canadian tariff board's recommendation is incomprehensible,-
That is the recommendation which is embodied in this resolution. I continue:
-especially at a time when the British share of the Canadian woollens market has been stable while the foreign share has been rapidly increasing.

The president of the Huddersfield chamber of commerce, which is in the very heart of the British woollen industry, said at the same time:
The recommendation of the tariff board-
Which is now the policy of the government. I continue:
-is not only disappointing, but inexplicable. Both the British and Canadian governments are expressing a desire to encourage trade between the two countries. It is not an encouragement when an increased duty is recommended on one of our largest exports.
Therefore, this matter is not considered as one of no importance in the United Kingdom especially, as I say, on the eve of the commonwealth economic conference. For this reason, and because it is not going to give any substantial help to the Canadian industry, and it is not meant to save the Canadian industry, as the tariff board report states very frankly, because, in negotiating with other countries under the M.F.N. clause, especially Italy, we can get ourselves into trouble in regard to exports from this country; for these and for a good many other reasons which I may have an opportunity to refer to on another occasion, I cannot support this resolution.
